newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten opposes China on Hong Kong schoolbooks.
newsitem.headline: Patten opposes China on Hong Kong schoolbooks.

text.p: Beijing was wrong to suggest Hong Kong schoolbooks may have to be revised after the British colony's return to China later this year, Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Monday.

"The Joint Declaration and the Basic Law guarantee Hong Kong's autonomy in educational matters after 1997," Patten said, referring to the Sino-British diplomatic accord on the handover and the territory's future China-drawn constitution.
"They are clear that educational policies are to be set by the (Hong Kong government), and not to be vetted for political correctness by Chinese officials," he said in a statement.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said earlier on Monday that Hong Kong schoolbooks that do not conform with China's principles should be revised after the handover.
Some textbooks went against the Basic Law and the "One Country, Two Systems" principle designed to let the territory keep its capitalist ways after the handover, Qian said.

"The contents of some textbooks currently used in Hong Kong do not accord with history or reality, are not suited to the changes after 1997, contradict the spirit of 'One Country Two Systems' and the Basic Law, and must be revised," he said.

Qian, speaking to the National People's Congress, China's parliament, gave no details of which schoolbooks would have to be changed or in what way they contradicted the Basic Law or were otherwise unsuitable.
Patten said Qian's comments were disturbing, and suggested the foreign minister should make clear what he meant.
"Naturally, school children need to be taught after 1997 about their new sovereign power, about the Joint Declaration, the Basic Law and One Country, Two Systems. This has already begun.
"But if Mr Qian is suggesting more than this, his statement raises some disturbing questions," he said.
Patten said the Joint Declaration and the Basic Law said nothing about rewriting history books.
"In a free society, teachers are not told what facts they can teach and what facts it is politically wrong for them to teach," he said.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 under a Sino-British accord that lets the territory keep its capitalist system and a "high degree" of autonomy for 50 years.
